t: Ge'ez was the language of the Kingdom of Aksum, carved on stone from the 4th century in a script made for it, which today also writes Amharic, Tigrinya and most other languages of Ethiopia.
Its Bible of 81 books, translated mostly from Greek in the first century of the Aksumite church, keeps the only complete text of the Book of Enoch.

No longer a living language by the 14th century, it remained Ethiopia’s official written language until the 19th, much like Medieval Latin in Europe, and is still the liturgical language of the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches and the Beta Israel.
dyk: The Apostolic Tradition, an early Christian text attributed to Hippolytus of Rome, is lost in its original Greek; its Ge'ez translation, made in the late 5th century, is the best surviving witness to it.
ev: Aksum becomes Christian under King Ezana, and surviving Ge'ez literature begins
The Hawulti obelisk at Matara is inscribed with the oldest known example of the Ge'ez script
The Aksumite Collection of liturgical, theological, synodal and historical texts is translated from Greek, late in the century
Ge'ez inscriptions in South Arabia record the conquests of Kaleb of Axum, the king who conquered Himyar
The Kebra Nagast, “Glory of the Kings”, retells the story of the Queen of Sheba, Solomon and their son Menelik I
The Fetha Negest, “Laws of the Kings”, is translated into Ge'ez; it serves as Ethiopia’s supreme law until 1931
Enbaqom writes the expanded Ge'ez version of his Anqasa Amin, “Gate of the Faith”, a classic of later Ge'ez literature
Ge'ez ceases to be the official written language of Ethiopia

f.family: Semitic: a South Semitic language; on another view, part of an independent Ethio-Semitic branch, in its northern half with Tigrinya and Tigre
f.script: Ethiopic, the Ge'ez abugida (called fidäl in Amharic and Tigrinya), developed for the language and read left to right; early inscriptions also in the South Arabian script, from the 4th century
f.earliest: Inscriptions of the Kingdom of Aksum from as early as the 4th century, about a dozen long and over 200 short; the oldest known example of the script on the Hawulti obelisk at Matara, Eritrea, tentatively c. 400; the oldest manuscript, the second Garima Gospel, of the 5th or 6th century
f.status: No longer spoken in daily life (no longer a living language by the 14th century); the main liturgical language of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches, the Ethiopian and Eritrean Catholic Churches and the Beta Israel, used in prayer and public celebrations
